There is substantial psycholinguistic evidence that skilled reading involves morphological analysis, whereby morphologically complex words like teacher are recognised via constituent morphemes {teach}+{-er}. The ability to recognise morphemes is vital as it allows readers to interpret both familiar and unfamiliar words. However, over 50% of the evidence for this claim comes from studies of suffixation in English, where morphemes typically have a relatively consistent surface form across exemplars (clean in cleaner, cleanliness; -ed in walked, jumped). item.title: Conventionality and transparency in human language
item.dc:creator: Sihan Chen
Antonio Benítez-Burraco
item.description:
Sihan Chen; Antonio Benítez-Burraco · PsyArXiv

The most distinctive feature of language is perhaps the ability to produce and comprehend utterances that have never been said before. This requires language to be transparent: comprehenders can infer the meaning of an utterance based on its components and the rules used to combine them. However, arbitrary associations between form and meaning (conventionality) are ubiquitous in language, despite them being difficult to learn. This is true for words, but also for many utterances. Why is this the case? In this paper, we propose languages balance conventionality and transparency by minimizing the communication and learning cost. item.description:
Andreas Lind; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall · PsyArXiv

Spontaneous speech is full of false starts, rephrasing, and speech errors. Speakers’ ability to detect errors and other problems in their own speech is commonly explained by monitoring mechanisms that rely on pre-articulatory representations, production states, or derivative predictions. We develop an alternative, cue-integrative account in which verbal self-monitoring is a natural consequence of what we have previously termed self-comprehension: speakers’ integration of contextual and sensory information to understand their own unfolding speech without requiring that meaning or intention be fully specified before articulation. Towards the end of their first year of life, infants learn to ignore variation in sounds not present, or not functional, in their ambient language. Specifically, overly specified word representations are thought to give way to others with which learners can cope better with indexical variation, such as voice and affect, which are not relevant to word identity. This developmental change may help infants in their second year to more efficiently process the ambient language and thus make rapid gains in vocabulary. item.dc:creator: Alejandrina Cristia
Yasuyo MINAGAWA
Natalia Egorova-Brumley

Emmanuel Dupoux
item.description:
Alejandrina Cristia; Yasuyo MINAGAWA; Natalia Egorova-Brumley; Judit Gervain; Lucas Filippin; Dominique Cabrol; Emmanuel Dupoux · PsyArXiv

The present study investigated the neural correlates of infant discrimination of very similar linguistic varieties (Quebecois and Parisian French) using functional Near InfraRed Spectroscopy. In line with previous behavioral and electrophysiological data, there was no evidence that 3-month-olds discriminated the two regional accents, whereas 5-month-olds did, with the locus of discrimination in left anterior perisylvian regions. These neuroimaging results suggest that a developing language network relying crucially on left perisylvian cortices sustains infants’ discrimination of similar linguistic varieties within this early period of infancy.

Determining the onset of experimental effects in timeseries data is central to psycholinguistics, because onset timing constrains theories about when different types of linguistic information become available during language processing. Psycholinguistic tools that estimate psychological symptoms from language alone aim to provide unobtrusive assessments without needing questionnaires or clinicians. Researchers largely assume that these assessments function equivalently across demographic groups. We tested this assumption in a racially diverse sample of U.S. adults (N = 1,685; Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, White) who described their mental health and completed standard symptom questionnaires. Research on predictive processing has shown that listeners anticipate upcoming linguistic information using linguistic cues, such as verb meaning. Beyond information in the input, listeners’ prediction can also be influenced by top-down control, such as goals and strategies developed in response to a given task. However, it is unclear to what extent evaluations of task relevance modulate top-down control of prediction. item.description:
Shervin Nosrati; Tyler Marghetis · PsyArXiv

When people think spatially, they adopt a frame of reference (egocentric or allocentric). People within a community often rely on the same frame of reference, but there is considerable variation between communities. How are these norms of spatial thinking transmitted? Linguistic relativity posits that they are transmitted through language; evidence for this account is mixed. We investigate a complementary mechanism, gestural relativity, whereby norms of spatial thinking are transmitted by gestures that express spatial information. item.description:
Louis Teitelbaum; Almog Simchon · PsyArXiv

Word counts or relative frequencies (e.g. the number of self-related words as a proportion of total words in a text) are routinely analyzed as dependent variables in the behavioral sciences. We demonstrate that conventional methods of analyzing word counts in this way are likely to lead to false positives, especially when text length varies between levels of the predictor variable. We performed Monte Carlo simulations to assess type I error rates for a wide range of affective and linguistic constructs across 9 datasets as well as known generative models, using 126 candidate statistical methods. Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas. This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -- the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together. However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature. Longitudinal learner corpus research (LCR) has grown substantially in recent years, resulting in richness and variety in study designs, analyses, and findings. Yet its design, measurement, and analysis practices have not been systematically assessed. To address this gap, this review synthesizes 120 longitudinal learner corpus studies published between 1996 and 2025, identified through systematic database searches and supplementary searching of the Learner Corpus Bibliography. Human language comprehension is remarkably robust---we are good at grasping what speakers and writers intend and can even understand them when their productions are not perfectly well-formed. item.title: Color Vision for Human Factors Engineering: When Color Helps, When It Hurts, and for Whom
item.dc:creator: David Henry Peterzell
item.description:
David Henry Peterzell · PsyArXiv

Color vision serves everyday tasks, from judging food and reading skin to segmenting scenes and reading signs, displays, and data. Designers use color in safety codes, interfaces, visualizations, lighting, and interiors, but practice often outruns evidence. I review when color helps, when it hurts, and for whom. Color helps when it carries information that luminance and form do not, as in judging ripeness, guiding search, and supporting scene memory. It hurts at isoluminance, in fine detail, in clutter or conflict, in non-uniform colormaps, and when it is the only carrier of critical information. Mental health shapes the progression and content of thought.
